0.0.n: Together with から, this sets the starting point as the present.

0.1.n: Marks a starting point in time; 今から introduces what happens next.

0.3.n: Refers to a recent time before speaking.

0.4.n: Describes the small amount of makeup applied.

0.5.n: Past form of 化粧する, with the polite-sounding prefix お.

0.6.n: Sentence-ending の gives a casual explanatory tone.

1.0.n: Combines with 早く to mean earlier than the actual time.

1.1.n: The adverb form of 早い describes when she intended to do it.

1.2.n: The intention form of やる; with と思った, it expresses what she planned to do.

1.3.n: Marks やろう as the thought reported by 思った.

1.4.n: Past form of 思う; here it describes an earlier intention.

1.5.n: Short for explanatory の in んだけど, introducing background for the contrast.

1.6.n: The plain form of です completes the explanatory expression んだ before けど.

1.7.n: Connects her intention with the contrasting result.

1.9.n: An expressive word describing hectic activity, not literal flapping here.

1.10.n: Links her hectic state to the reason she could not do it.

1.11.n: Past negative form of できる, expressing inability.

2.0.n: A casual connector that picks up the story from the previous sentence.

2.2.n: This subtitle chunk contains 今 plus the first character of やっと; it is not the expression 今や.

2.3.n: This chunk completes やっと, which starts in the previous chunk and suggests a delay or difficulty.

2.4.n: Describes the amount of makeup, with だけ emphasizing its smallness.

2.5.n: Limits the amount expressed by ちょっと.

2.6.n: The て-form of 化粧する connects this action to the next part of the story.

3.0.n: With から, it introduces the next action she is about to take.

3.1.n: Marks the present as the starting point in 今から.

3.2.n: A person's name, written in katakana.

3.3.n: Marks Hannah as the person being picked up.

3.4.n: The て-form of ピックアップする connects the pickup to the following plans.

4.0.n: The name of a holiday, written as a katakana borrowing.

4.1.n: A conversational form of という, used to introduce a name.

4.2.n: Stands for a thing or occasion bearing the name just given.

4.3.n: Marks the named occasion as what exists in the following あって.

4.4.n: The て-form of ある links the existence of this occasion to the next explanation.

5.0.n: Refers back to St. Patrick's Day.

5.1.n: Links the holiday to its associated event.

5.2.n: A katakana borrowing referring to the holiday-related gathering or activity.

5.3.n: Marks the event as the setting for making crafts.

5.4.n: The thing to be made; conversational speech leaves out the object marker を here.

5.5.n: Casual shortening of 作らなきゃ; together with いけない, it expresses an obligation to make something.

5.6.n: The linking form of いけない completes the obligation expression and connects it to the shopping plan.

5.8.n: Points back to the craft already mentioned.

5.9.n: Literally クラフト names the craft; here the shopping context suggests the materials needed to make it.

5.10.n: Marks the craft supplies as what they will buy.

5.11.n: A person's name; と identifies her as the shopping companion.

5.12.n: Marks Hannah as the person accompanying the speaker.

5.13.n: The stem of 買う, used before に行く to state the purpose of going.

5.14.n: Marks buying as the purpose of the trip.

5.15.n: The て-form of 行く links this shopping trip to the rest of the plans.

6.0.n: A person's name, written in katakana.

6.1.n: Joins Nina and Gina as a pair.

6.2.n: A person's name, written in katakana.

6.3.n: Makes Nina and Gina the topic; they are the people Taiga will pick up.

6.4.n: Shows that the speaker is not completely certain about this plan.

6.5.n: This chunk is the beginning of the person's name たいが, completed by the next chunk.

6.6.n: This が completes the name たいが; it is not a particle.

6.7.n: Marks Taiga as the person doing the pickup.

6.8.n: A casual shortening of ピックアップ, combined with して to describe collecting people.

6.9.n: The て-form of する turns ピック into an action and links it to eating.

6.10.n: Here ご飯 refers to food or a meal, not specifically rice; the object marker を is omitted.

6.11.n: 食べて is the linking form of 食べる; って presents the preceding activities as the rough plan.

6.12.n: With って, 感じ loosely summarizes how things are expected to go.

6.13.n: A polite sentence ending after the otherwise casual description.

0.lit: From now… a little while ago, I put on a little makeup, you see.
0.tip: 今から trails off before the speaker switches to describing something she already did.

1.lit: I thought I would do it earlier, but being rushed, I couldn't.
1.tip: A verb's intention form plus と思った expresses what someone planned to do.

2.lit: So, now, finally, I put on just a little makeup, and…
2.tip: Read 今やっと as 今 plus やっと, despite the subtitle chunks splitting it incorrectly.

3.lit: From now, picking up Hannah, and…
3.tip: A て-form can link planned future actions, not just actions already completed.

4.lit: There is something called St. Patrick's Day, and…
4.tip: っていうのがある is a conversational way to introduce something by name.

5.lit: At that event, we have to make a craft, so I go with Hannah to buy that craft, and…
5.tip: 買いに行く means going in order to buy: the verb stem plus に marks the trip's purpose.

6.lit: As for Nina and Gina, probably Taiga picks them up, they eat a meal—that's the general plan.
6.tip: って感じです loosely wraps up a description: that's roughly how things will go.
